title: Maximum-Length Distinct-Character Window

notes: Use a sliding-window with a map of last-seen indices to achieve O(n) time.
If your language's character set is large, use a hash map rather than a fixed-size array unless appropriate.
Do not normalize case unless explicitly required.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, printable ASCII symbols and spaces
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of arguments, e.g. ["abcabcbb"]
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialized integer (length of longest substring without repeating characters)

sampleTestCases.explanation: A longest duplicate-free contiguous segment is "abc", which has length 3.
Every contiguous segment of length greater than 1 repeats the character 'b'.
The segment "wke" contains three distinct characters. "pwke" is not contiguous.

content.problemStatement:
You receive a string s. Identify the largest length of a contiguous substring in which every character appears no more than once, and output that length.

Characters are matched exactly (case-sensitive). The input may contain letters, digits, printable ASCII punctuation, and spaces. An empty string has answer 0.

Aim for O(n) time using a sliding window and a last-seen-position table or hash map.

hidden.label: Quotes and backslashes require correct JSON escaping
Repeated character inside otherwise long window
Alternating repeated character with unique separators
Maximum-length constraint with the full printable ASCII alphabet

notes: All hidden test cases are concrete strings or deterministic JavaScript-generated strings using only printable ASCII characters and spaces.
The checker compares the returned integer to the expected length.
Solutions should run in O(n) time and use O(min(n, alphabet_size)) auxiliary space.
The C implementation uses a 256-entry last-seen table because the input is restricted to ASCII characters.
The other reference implementations use hash maps because the allowed alphabet is small but language-neutral.
solution.approach: Sliding-window with last-seen index map: maintain two pointers (left, right). Expand right; when a character repeats inside the window, move left to lastSeen[char] + 1 if that is greater than current left. Track max window length as right - left + 1. Use a hash map from character to last index.

better.complexity: O(n^2) time and O(alphabet_size) auxiliary space.
better.description: For each starting position, extend the substring until the first duplicate using a set. This avoids rebuilding the set for every endpoint, but still examines O(n^2) candidate extensions in the worst case.

optimal.complexity: O(n) time and O(min(n, alphabet_size)) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Maintain a sliding window [left, right] containing no duplicate characters. Store each character's most recent index. When the current character was last seen inside the window, jump left to lastSeen[char] + 1. Each index is processed a constant number of times.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n^2) time and O(alphabet_size) auxiliary space when each start position is extended incrementally.
bruteForce.description: Enumerate every substring and check whether its characters are all distinct. This is correct but can take O(n^3) time with a fresh set for each substring, or O(n^2) with incremental checking.

hints: Use a hash map to store the last index where each character was seen.
Maintain a left pointer for the current window; when a repeat is found, move left to lastSeen + 1.
Track the maximum window length while scanning once from left to right.
followUps: How would you adapt the algorithm if characters were Unicode and the string length is large?
How would you return the substring itself (not just the length) while preserving O(n) time?
learningObjectives: Hash map usage for last-seen positions
similarProblems: Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters
